title_th: การเช็คอิน/เช็คเอาต์ (แขก)
recycles: telling the time / dates ('until Friday', 'half past seven')
'How much is it?' / paying by card or cash
spelling your name and giving personal details
clarification requests ('Sorry, could you say that again?')
register: Polite-neutral service English: friendly, short sentences, 'please' and 'thanks' on every request; staff may be casual, guest stays courteous but direct.

words_in_context: I have a reservation — booked online
targets.why_it_matters_here: Thai speakers drop or unrelease final consonants, so 'key card' becomes 'key car' (the clerk hears a parking question), 'I booked online' becomes 'I book online' (sounds like you want to book now, not that you already have a reservation), and 'three nights' becomes 'three night' — which staff often hear as 'tonight', so you get charged for one night and lose your room on day two.

Teen/ty confusion at a front desk costs money and time: 'fifteen' heard as 'fifty' turns a $15 late-checkout fee into $50 on your bill, and room 'three-fourteen' heard as 'three-forty' sends you to the wrong door with a card that won't open it. Final -n in 'thirteen' and stress on the second syllable are what make the difference audible.

chunk_drills.label: Announcing yourself at check-in
chunk_drills.pattern: I have a reservation. The name's ___.
examples: I have a reservation. The name's Somchai.
I have a booking for tonight. The name's Nan.
I booked online — two nights, under Wongsa.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Present simple + possessive 'the name's'; recycles spelling your name and giving personal details.

chunk_drills.label: Saying how long you're staying (final -s and -ts)
examples: Three nights, from Friday to Monday.
One night only.
Two nights, checking out on the fifteenth.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Countable nouns with plural -s; recycles dates and days of the week.

chunk_drills.label: The money questions
chunk_drills.pattern: Is ___ included? / How much is ___? / Can I pay by ___?
examples: Is breakfast included?
How much is the deposit?
Is there an extra charge for late checkout?
Can I pay by card?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Yes/no questions with 'is there'; recycles 'How much?' and prices.

chunk_drills.label: Asking about time (checkout, breakfast, storage)
examples: What time is checkout?
What time does breakfast start?
How late can I leave my bags?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Wh- questions with 'do/does'; recycles clock times.

chunk_drills.label: Polite requests at the desk
examples: Could I have a wake-up call at six?
Can I leave my bags here?
Could I get a receipt, please?
Could I have a room on a higher floor?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Modal 'could/can' for requests; recycles polite service language.

chunk_drills.label: Checking a number back (repair strategy)
examples: Sorry — thirteen or thirty?
So that's room three-one-four, right?
Fifteen dollars, not fifty?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Tag-style confirmation questions; recycles clarification requests and numbers.

chunk_drills.label: Reporting a problem calmly
chunk_drills.pattern: I think there's a mistake — I didn't ___.
examples: I think there's a mistake — I didn't use the minibar.
Sorry, I booked a twin room, not a double.
The air con isn't working. Could someone have a look?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Past simple negative 'didn't + verb'; recycles describing a problem.

listening_items.audio_text: You're in room three-fourteen, on the third floor. The lift is behind you.
listening_items.question: What is the room number and the floor?

listening_items.audio_text: Checkout is at eleven, but late checkout until two is fifteen dollars.
listening_items.question: How much is late checkout?

listening_items.audio_text: Sorry, the room isn't ready yet. Could you come back at half past one?
listening_items.question: What should the guest do?
listening_items.answer: Come back at 1:30 — the room isn't ready

listening_items.audio_text: Hi, this is reception. We have your booking for two nights, arriving on the thirteenth.
listening_items.question: How many nights, and what date do they arrive?

listening_items.answer: Until 6 p.m.; bring the luggage tag

listening_items.audio_text: There's a deposit of fifty on the card, and we release it after checkout.
listening_items.question: How much is the deposit and when do you get it back?

guided_roleplay.learner_role: Hotel guest arriving alone with a three-night booking, then checking out the next-to-last morning with an early-evening flight
flow: 1. Arrive at reception, greet, and say you have a reservation with your name.
2. Confirm the details out loud: how many nights, what room type.
3. Hand over your passport and answer 'How will you be paying?'
4. Ask two service questions: 'Is breakfast included?' and 'What time is checkout?'
5. Repeat the room number and floor back to the clerk to confirm.
6. (Check-out day) Say you're checking out and give your room number.
7. Look at the bill and query one item you don't recognise.
8. Pay, ask for a receipt, and ask to leave your bags until the evening.
9. Confirm the tag number and the pick-up time.
sentence_frames: I have a reservation. The name's ___.
I think there's a mistake — I didn't ___.
Could I get a receipt, please?
Can I leave my bags here until ___?

free_roleplay.ai_persona: Friendly but busy front-desk receptionist at a mid-range city hotel. Uses short, natural service phrases ('No worries', 'Bear with me', 'All done'), speaks at normal speed, and says numbers quickly the first time — but will slow down and repeat if the learner asks.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Sticks to the standard script: confirms the booking, asks for passport and card, gives the room number, floor, breakfast time and checkout time, and answers 'Is breakfast included?' directly. At check-out, reads the total, takes the card, gives a receipt, and agrees to store bags.
b1_curveballs: The room isn't ready yet — offers 1:30 pick-up and asks if the guest wants to leave bags in the meantime.
The booking shows a twin room, not the double the guest booked — the guest has to explain the mistake.
Asks for a deposit: 'We'll put a hold of fifty on your card, released after checkout.'
The bill has an extra minibar or breakfast charge the guest didn't use.
Says numbers fast and slightly ambiguously ('three-fourteen', 'fifteen') and only clarifies if asked.
Luggage storage closes at six but the guest's flight means coming back at seven — needs negotiating.
Offers a late checkout for a fee and asks 'Do you want it?' — the guest must decide and confirm the price.

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Stated the reservation and gave name, nights and room type without being asked twice
Asked at least two service questions (breakfast / checkout time / Wi-Fi / bag storage)
Confirmed key numbers back to the clerk (room number, price, tag number, time)
Used a clarification or repair move when a number or instruction was unclear ('Sorry — thirteen or thirty?')
Completed check-out: understood the total, paid, and asked for a receipt
Register stayed polite-neutral — requests with 'Could I / Can I', thanks at the end, no bare imperatives
Pronunciation: final consonants audible in 'card', 'bags', 'nights', 'booked'; teen/ty numbers distinguishable
Handled an off-script problem (wrong charge, room not ready, bag pick-up after closing) and reached a solution without breaking down

register_culture_note.en: Hotel front desks run on short, friendly, transactional English. You do not need long apologetic sentences — 'Hi, I have a reservation, the name's Nan' is perfect. Two habits matter more than grammar: (1) repeat numbers back ('So that's room three-fourteen?'), which staff expect and find helpful, and (2) ask about money and rules up front — deposit, breakfast, checkout time, late-checkout fee. Querying a charge on your bill is completely normal and is not treated as an accusation; say 'I think there's a mistake' rather than staying silent and paying.

do_dont.prefer: Could I have the key card, please?

do_dont.avoid: I book online. (past event said with no final -d)
do_dont.prefer: I booked online — I have a reservation.

do_dont.avoid: Fifty? (when you mean fifteen, with flat stress)
Silently paying a charge you don't recognise.
do_dont.prefer: I think there's a mistake — I didn't use the minibar.

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: In Thailand it can feel more comfortable to accept what the desk says and sort out problems quietly, especially over a small amount of money. In most international hotels the opposite is expected: staff assume guests will check the bill and speak up on the spot, and once you have paid and left, fixing a wrong charge is much harder. Asking 'Could you check that again?' at the desk is a routine, low-conflict request — the clerk will usually thank you for catching it.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can check in by saying I have a reservation, giving my name, and confirming how many nights.
I can understand and repeat back my room number, floor, breakfast time and checkout time.
I can ask 'Is breakfast included?', 'What time is checkout?' and 'Can I pay by card?'
I can ask to leave my bags at the desk and confirm when I'll come back.
I can query an item on my bill politely and reach an agreement about what I owe.
I can handle an unexpected situation at the desk — room not ready, wrong room type, deposit, late pick-up — and negotiate an alternative.
My final consonants in 'card', 'bags', 'nights' and 'booked' are audible, and staff hear the difference between thirteen and thirty.
